# FIG. 2

A flat schematic diagram of one connector channel in plain black line work on white, no shading and no text. All line work stays well inside the drawing area, clear of the filing margins.

A dashed rectangle occupies the left and central portion of the drawing area, representing the first connector channel.

A solid vertical line enters from above, crosses the top side of the dashed rectangle and continues downward inside it, as the incoming branch supply. A contactor interrupts this line, shown schematically as a small empty square outline straddling the line, the line meeting the outline above and below.

Below the contactor the line resumes, turns right and runs horizontally to the right side of the dashed rectangle. A small square outline straddles this horizontal run and represents the connector current sensor, shown schematically, the run continuing to the right of it. The run reaches an empty rectangular block straddling the right side of the dashed rectangle, the vehicle connector, shown schematically.

An empty rectangular block sits in the lower region of the dashed rectangle, below the horizontal run, representing the control-pilot interface.

Right of the dashed rectangle a larger rounded rectangle represents an electric vehicle, shown schematically. A short solid line runs from the right side of the vehicle connector block to the left side of the rounded rectangle, and a second from the right side of the control-pilot interface block to the lower side of the vehicle connector block.

A solid horizontal line enters from the left and crosses the left side of the dashed rectangle in its lower region, as the isolated local bus. Inside the rectangle it branches two ways: one branch to the left side of the control-pilot interface block and a second upward to the contactor outline. A separate solid line enters from the left above the bus line, crosses the left side of the dashed rectangle and runs to the square outline representing the connector current sensor, carrying the connector current sensor report to the edge controller.

The part names listed below are semantic identifiers only and do not appear as drawing text.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 108 isolated local bus: leader ends on the bus line left of the dashed rectangle.
- 120 first connector channel: leader ends on the dashed rectangle.
- 122 contactor: leader ends on the square outline straddling the vertical line.
- 124 connector current sensor: leader ends on the square outline straddling the horizontal run.
- 126 control-pilot interface: leader ends well inside the lower block within the dashed rectangle.
- 128 vehicle connector: leader ends well inside the block straddling the right side.
- 130 electric vehicle: leader ends well inside the rounded rectangle.

1	FIG. 1 shows a charging installation 100 in which several electric vehicles are charged from one electrical branch. A branch conductor 102 is the conductor of that electrical branch and has a branch current limit, that is, an allowable aggregate current of the branch conductor 102, and a reference below to the electrical branch is a reference to the branch supplied by the branch conductor 102. The branch current limit is lower than a sum of the current ratings of the vehicle connectors served by the branch conductor 102, so that the connectors cannot all deliver their rated current at the same time and the aggregate current is governed by control rather than by the rating of any one connector.
2	
3	A first connector channel 120 and a second connector channel 140 are connected to the branch conductor 102 in parallel. The description of the first connector channel 120 applies to each further connector channel connected to the branch conductor 102, the second connector channel 140 being of the same construction. A non-charging load 118 is also connected to the branch conductor 102 and represents the equipment of the site that shares the branch and whose current the controller does not command.
4	
5	A branch current sensor 104 is arranged on the branch conductor 102 upstream of the contactors of the connector channels and measures a branch current, that is, the total current carried by the branch conductor 102. Because the branch current sensor 104 is upstream of every connector channel and of the non-charging load 118, its measurement is independent of the measurements made within the connector channels. The branch current sensor 104 is treated as an independent safety input throughout this description.
6	
7	An edge controller 106, also referred to herein as a controller, is coupled to the branch current sensor 104 and is coupled to the connector channels by an isolated local bus 108. The isolated local bus 108 carries the assigned current limits, the contactor commands and the pilot reports between the edge controller 106 and the connector channels. The edge controller 106 further receives the connector current reported by the connector current sensor of each connector channel.

1	Parking structures, fleet depots, workplaces and multi unit dwellings commonly install several electric vehicle connectors on a single electrical branch. The conductors, overcurrent device and upstream transformer capacity of that branch are sized for an aggregate current that is lower, and often much lower, than the sum of the individual current ratings of the connectors served by it. The installation therefore depends on a control function that continuously divides the branch capacity among the connectors that are in use, rather than on the physical rating of any one connector.
2	
3	A control function of this kind ordinarily issues a current limit to each vehicle over a control pilot signalling interface. The limit is advisory in the sense that it is a request addressed to equipment that the site operator does not own and cannot inspect. A vehicle may respond slowly, may respond only in coarse steps, may hold a previous current for an interval after a new limit is signalled, or may not follow the signalled limit at all. Auxiliary equipment on the same branch, such as lighting, ventilation, elevators or refrigeration, draws current that the charging control function does not command and that changes without notice. A control function that computes an allocation and then assumes the allocation has taken effect can therefore hold the branch above its rated aggregate current while every connector believes it is compliant, with the overcurrent device of the branch as the only remaining protection.
4	Site controllers of this class also depend on a network connection to a remote management service for schedules, tariffs and driver authorization. Connectivity in a below grade parking structure or a remote depot is intermittent. A controller that treats loss of connectivity as a reason to stop charging strands vehicles that were already authorized, while a controller that treats loss of connectivity as permission to charge without restraint abandons the branch limit that the last accepted configuration established, and abandons the accounting record that billing depends on.
5	
6	A further difficulty arises at installation. The connector identifier used by the control function, the physical contactor that energizes a connector and the current sensing channel that measures it are joined by field wiring performed once, often by a contractor who does not operate the equipment afterwards. If that wiring map is recorded incorrectly, the control function will deliver a computed current limit to one connector while measuring another. Every subsequent verification appears to succeed, because the two errors are consistent with one another, and the fault is discovered only when the branch overcurrent device operates or when a vehicle receives a limit that was intended for a different vehicle.
7	
8	There remains a need for a controller that treats the aggregate current of the branch as a measured quantity, verified independently of the per connector measurements and independently of any vehicle response, and that converts an unanswered current reduction into a bounded, ordered and recoverable removal of load rather than into an uncontrolled trip of the branch overcurrent device.
9

1	An apparatus controls charging of electric vehicles at a plurality of vehicle connectors supplied by a common electrical branch whose branch current limit is lower than a sum of the current ratings of those vehicle connectors. Each connector channel of the apparatus includes a contactor connected between the electrical branch and a respective vehicle connector, a connector current sensor arranged to measure a connector current delivered through that vehicle connector, and a control-pilot interface, and each connector channel is associated with a local connector identifier. A branch current sensor is arranged to measure a branch current in the electrical branch upstream of the contactors of the plurality of connector channels, so that the aggregate current of the branch is obtained from a measurement that is independent of the per connector measurements.
2	
3	A controller is coupled to the control-pilot interfaces, to the contactors and to the branch current sensor. The controller stores, for each active connector channel, a charging authorization, a requested current, a minimum sustaining current and an energy-deficit value. At each allocation interval of a succession of allocation intervals, the controller subtracts a measured non-charging branch load and a configurable safety reserve from the branch current limit to obtain an available charging current, assigns the minimum sustaining current from the available charging current to each active connector channel that can receive the minimum sustaining current, and distributes a remainder of the available charging current among the active connector channels according to the stored energy-deficit values, thereby obtaining an assigned current limit for each active connector channel. The controller sends the assigned current limit for each active connector channel through the control-pilot interface of that connector channel and verifies the connector current resulting from the assigned current limit with the connector current sensor of that connector channel.
4	
5	The branch current sensor serves as an independent safety input. Responsive to the measured branch current remaining above the branch current limit for a verification interval after a reduced pilot command has been sent, the controller opens the contactors of the plurality of connector channels one at a time in a stored shedding order until the measured branch current is below the branch current limit. Load is therefore removed in a bounded and predetermined sequence, and only to the extent that the measured branch current shows the removal to be necessary.
6	
7	In further aspects, a contactor is not reclosed until the connector current sensor of its connector channel reports zero connector current, the control-pilot interface of that connector channel reports a connected vehicle, and a randomized recovery delay has expired, so that connector channels that were shed together do not restore load simultaneously. A welded-contactor condition is recorded when the connector current of a connector channel remains above a leakage threshold after an open command has been issued to the contactor of that connector channel, whereupon the controller inhibits the contactors of the other connector channels on the electrical branch and operates a local fault indicator.
8	
9	In further aspects, the controller receives remote schedules and remote authorizations through a network interface while holding a signed local authorization token and a last accepted branch limit in nonvolatile memory. During a network outage the controller continues already authorized charging sessions subject to the last accepted branch limit and subject to the branch current sensing described above, and does not start a charging session at a newly connected vehicle connector unless the signed local authorization token authorizes the local connector identifier of that connector channel and has not expired. Meter records are appended to a tamper-evident local sequence and uploaded when communication returns.
10	
11	In a further aspect, a service input permits an installer to associate the local connector identifiers with the physical contactors by commanding one low-energy pilot transition at a time and confirming the connector current sensor that responds, the association being stored only after the responding connector current sensor agrees with the commanded connector channel, so that a field wiring error cannot cause an assigned current limit to be applied to the wrong vehicle connector.
12	
13	Corresponding methods are also disclosed.
